en: Oṃ, homage to all the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas, residing in the infinite and boundless world-systems of the ten directions, belonging to the past, future, and present.
Homage to Amitābha. Homage to Amitāyus. Homage to the one whose nature is a mine of inconceivable qualities. Homage to you, O Sage, the Victor Amitābha.
Out of compassion for you, I go to Sukhāvatī—
that delightful Sukhāvatī with its groves variegated by gold, adorned by the sons of the Sugata.
Thus, I shall go to that city of the wise one of renowned fame, which is a collection of many jewels of virtues.
Thus have I heard:
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great community of monks.

Together with thirty-two thousand bhikṣus, all of whom were arhats, whose taints were exhausted, who were free from afflictions, who had lived the holy life, and whose minds were well-liberated through right knowledge.
By those who have exhausted the thousands of fetters of existence, who have attained their own goal,
who are victorious,
who have reached supreme self-mastery, and who have attained tranquility;
by those with minds well-liberated and wisdom well-liberated, great nāgas, possessed of the six superknowledges,
having attained mastery, meditating on the eight liberations, having acquired the powers, and renowned for their superknowledges;
by the elders, the great śrāvakas. Namely:
by Ājñāta Kauṇḍinya;
and Aśvajit,
and Bāṣpa,
and Mahānāman;
And by Bhadrajit, and by Yaśodeva, and by Vimala.
And with Subāhu, and Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra,
and Gavāmpati;
and with Uruvilvākāśyapa,
Nadīkāśyapa, and Bhadrakāśyapa;
And by Kumārakāśyapa, and by Mahākāśyapa,
and by Śāriputra.
and with Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Mahākapphiṇa, and Mahācunda;
And by Aniruddha, and by Rādha,
and by Nandika.
and Kimpila, and Subhūti,
and Revata.
and by Khadiravanika, and by Vakkula, and by Svāgata, and by Amogharāja;
And Pārāyaṇika, and Pantha, and Cūḷapantha,
and Nanda.
And by Rāhula, and by the Venerable Ānanda; and by these and other elder great śrāvakas who were well-known for their supernormal powers.
With the exception of one person, those practicing as learners (*śaikṣa*) still have further things to do; namely,
the Venerable Ānanda,
preceded by Maitreya.
and with a great many bodhisattva mahāsattvas.
Then, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, and placed his right knee upon the ground.
Bowing with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, he said this to the Blessed One:
"The faculties of you, Blessed One, are perfectly serene."
The color of his skin was completely pure, the complexion of his face was radiant and bright, shining with a golden luster,
just like the pale and perfectly clear autumnal cloudless sky.
It was pure and radiant with a golden luster. In just this way, the Blessed One’s faculties were serene,
and the color of his face was perfectly clear.
The color of his skin was pure, radiant with a golden luster. Blessed One, it was just like, for example, a coin made of Jambūnada gold.
It was thoroughly refined by the skilled smith Dakṣa, the son of a smith,
after being cast into the mouth of a furnace, and then placed upon white woolen blankets.
It is intensely pure,
cleansed, and radiant with a golden luster. In the very same way, the sense-faculties of the Blessed One are serene.
The color of his face is completely pure, the color of his skin is radiant and clear, glowing with a golden luster.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, I do not recall ever having known this before.
Formerly, even more so in the past, the faculties of the Tathāgata were thus serene,
and the color of his face was thus pure.
My complexion was purified and radiant with a golden glow. Then, Blessed One, this thought occurred to me:
"By means of the dwelling of a Buddha..."
Today the Tathāgata dwells thus:
by the dwelling of the Victor,
by the dwelling of omniscience.
"Indeed, today the Tathāgata dwells with the dwelling of a great nāga;
he clearly perceives the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones of the past, future, and present."
When this had been said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!
But why did those deities announce this matter to you?"

"Or rather, [do you know this] because the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, [know it], or do you understand it thus by means of your own present knowledge of investigation? When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Blessed One, it was not deities who informed me of this matter,
nor were it the Blessed Buddhas. Rather,"
Then, Blessed One, by means of my own knowledge from personal investigation, it occurs to me thus: "Today the Tathāgata dwells in the dwelling of a Buddha; he dwells in the dwelling of a Jina."
By means of the dwelling in omniscience and the dwelling of the Great Naga, the Tathāgata dwells today; [he dwells] with all the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, of the past, future, and present. P4
"he observes.
When this was said, the Blessed One spoke thus to the venerable Ānanda: "Excellent, excellent, Ānanda!"
Truly noble is your exertion, auspicious your inquiry, and excellent your eloquence,
for the benefit of many people.
You, Ānanda, have set out for the welfare of many people,
out of compassion for the world.
For the sake, welfare, and happiness of the great body of beings— both gods and humans—
it is well that you have asked the Tathāgata about this matter which ought to be inquired after.
"It is so, Ānanda; it is thus:
the knowledge and vision regarding the Tathāgatas, the Arhats, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, is immeasurable and incalculable."
Even as he bestows [these gifts], the wisdom of the Tathāgata is not impaired.
For what reason? Because, Ānanda, the Tathāgata possesses unimpeded knowledge and vision regarding causes.
If he so desired, Ānanda, the Tathāgata could remain for an eon, or even for a hundred eons, on a single alms-meal.
For a thousand eons, or a hundred thousand eons, or even up to a hundred thousand nayutas of koṭīs of eons; from that...
Furthermore, the faculties of the Tathāgata do not diminish; there is no change in the color of his face, nor is the complexion of his skin impaired. That...

For what reason? Because, Ānanda, the Tathāgata has attained the perfection of the gateways of meditative concentration. Ānanda, the appearance of perfectly awakened ones in the world is very difficult to encounter.
Just as the appearance of udumbara flowers in the world is extremely rare, even so is the appearance of Tathāgatas who desire the welfare of beings.
The appearance of those who desire the welfare of others, who are compassionate, and who have undertaken great compassion is extremely rare. Nevertheless, O noble Ānanda,
this is indeed the power of the Tathāgata himself.

It is well that you, for the sake of the appearance in the world of all teachers of the world and for the benefit of the bodhisattvas, the mahāsattvas, consider this matter to be one that should be asked of the Tathāgata.
"Therefore, Ānanda, listen well and attend closely;
I shall speak to you. "So be it, Blessed One," replied the Venerable Ānanda.
He gave his assent to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this to him: "In the past, Ānanda, long ago..."

"Ananda, in a time long past, incalculable, more than incalculable, vast, immeasurable, and inconceivable eons ago, at that time and on that occasion, there appeared in the world a Tathagata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha named Dīpaṃkara. Ananda, [of] Dīpaṃkara...

After him, even further back, there was a Tathāgata named Pratāpavān. After him, even further back, there was a Tathāgata named Prabhākara. After him, even further back, there was a Tathāgata named Candanagandha.
Thereafter, there appeared a Tathāgata named Sumerukalpa; likewise, one named Candrānana,
and one named Vimalānana.
One named Anupalipta, one named Vimalaprabha,
and one named Nāgābhibhū.
named Sūryānana,
named Girirājaghoṣa,
and named Sumerukūṭa;
named Suvarṇaprabhāsa, named Jyotiṣprabha, and named Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa;
named Brahmaghoṣa,
named Candrābhibhū, and named Sūryaghoṣa.
named [the Buddha] Muktakusumapratimaṇḍitaprabha,
named Śrīkūṭa,
and named Sāgaravarabuddhivikrīḍitābhijña.
named Varaprabha,
named Mahāgandharājanirbhāsa, and named Vyapagatakhilamalapratigha.
named Śūra-kūṭa,
named Ratna-jaha, and named Mahā-guṇadhara-buddhi-prāpta-abhijña.
named [the Tathāgata] Candrasūryajihmīkaraṇa, named [the Tathāgata] Uttaptavaiḍūryanirbhāsa,
and named [the Tathāgata] Cittadhārābuddhisaṃkusumitābhyudgata.
He was named Puṣpāvatīvanarājasaṃkusumitābhijña, named Puṣpākara, named Udakacandropama,
and named Avidyāndhakāravidhvaṃsanakara.
named Lokendra,
named Muktacchatrāpravāḍasadṛśa, and named Tiṣya.
the one named Dharmamativinanditarāja, the one named Siṃhasāgarakūṭavinanditarāja,
the one named Sāgaramerucandra, and Brahma—
The one named Svaranādābhinandin,
the one named Kusumasaṃbhava, and Prāptasena.
named Nāma, named Candrabhānu, named Merukūṭa, and named Candraprabha.
named Vimalanetra,
named Girirājaghoṣeśvara,
and named Kusumaprabha;
The one named Abhiprakīrṇa (Sprinkled with a Rain of Flowers),
the one named Ratnacchatra (Jewel Parasol), and the one named Padmavīthyupaśobhita (Adorned with Lotus Rows).
One named Tagaragandha, one named Ratnanirbhāsa,
and one named Nirmita.
named Mahāvyūha, named Vyapagatakhiladoṣa, and named Brahmaghoṣa;
Named "Showers of the Seven Jewels," named "Upholder of Great Virtues," and [scented with] the paste of *tamāla* leaves and sandalwood.
named Kusumābhijña, named Ajñānavidhvaṃsana, and named Keśarī;
The one named Muktacchatra,
the one named Suvarṇagarbha, and the one named Vaiḍūryagarbha.
One named Mahāketu,
one named Dharmaketu, and one named Ratnaśrī.
Named Narendro, named Lokendro, named Kāruṇiko.
named Lokasundara, named Brahmaketu, and named Dharmamati;
named Siṃha,
named Siṃhamati, and [the son] of Siṃhamati.
Ānanda, after that, even further beyond, a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Lokeśvararāja appeared in the world,
endowed with knowledge and conduct—
He is perfected, the Sugata, the knower of the world, the unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed.
He was the teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
Furthermore, Ānanda, of that Tathāgata, Arhat, and World-Chief King...
In the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One, there was a monk named Dharmākara,
who possessed supreme mindfulness.
He possessed [excellent] conduct, was endowed with wisdom, possessed supreme vigor,
and had sublime resolve.
Then, Ānanda, that monk Dharmākara rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder,
and placed his right knee upon the ground.
Having established [it], he bowed with palms joined toward where that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, was located.
Having paid homage to the Blessed One,
at that time he praised him to his face with these verses:
"O Amitaprabha!"
O you of infinite and equal wisdom,
no other radiance whatsoever shines here—
not the splendor of the sun-gems, nor the light of the moon.
Neither has he burned nor spoken in all these worlds. (1) Form too is infinite in the essence of beings,
and likewise the Buddha’s voice is of infinite resonance.
In this world, there is no other equal to you in terms of ethical discipline, meditative concentration, wisdom, and vigor.
You have attained a Dharma that is profound, vast, and subtle. (2)
The supreme Buddha was as inconceivable as the ocean.
Therefore, there was no arrogance on the part of the Teacher;
having abandoned the fault of stubbornness, he reached the further shore. (3)
Just as the excellent Buddha of infinite splendor, the king of lords of men, shines forth in all directions,
so shall I become a Buddha, a lord of the Dharma.
May I liberate all beings from old age and death.
Likewise, [may I establish them] in the supreme and most excellent generosity, self-restraint, discipline, patience, vigor, meditation, and concentration.
With these, I undertake the vows:
"I shall become a Buddha, a protector of all sentient beings.
(5) Many hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddhas... P8
Just as the sands of the Ganges are infinite,
so shall I worship all those incomparable Lords, seeking the supreme and auspicious awakening. (6)
I shall emit light everywhere throughout world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and even further into those infinite realms that lie beyond.
Thus, I shall exert such vigor.
My field shall be vast, supreme, and most excellent; here, in this conditioned world, it shall be the choice essence.
The incomparable bliss of the world-system of nirvāṇa,
and that I shall purify through the state of non-substantiality.
(8) Sentient beings gathered from the ten directions—
Having gone there, they will quickly flourish in happiness.
O Buddha, you are my authority and witness in this matter; I generate the desire for the power of unerring diligence. (9)
May those who know the world in the ten directions, possessing unimpeded wisdom, always recognize my mind;
may I always dwell even in the Avīci hell.
"I shall not turn back from the power of my vow. (10) Then, Ānanda, that monk Dharmākara, in the presence of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, [praised him] with these verses:
Having praised him, he said this:
"Blessed One, I am desirous of awakening to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
Again and again,
I generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
I dedicate it.
May the Blessed One teach me the Dharma well and in such a way that I may quickly awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment;
that I may become an incomparable Tathāgata in the world; and [may he grant] those to me...
"May the Blessed One proclaim the qualities by which I may take hold of the excellence of the array of virtues of a buddha-field. When this was said, Ānanda, he—
The Blessed One, the Tathāgata, the King of the Lords of the World, said this to that monk:
"In that case, monk, you yourself must take hold of the excellence of the array of ornaments and qualities of a buddha-field. He replied: "I do not..."
"Blessed One, I am willing. However, may the Blessed One himself describe the perfection of the array of qualities of the buddha-fields of other Tathāgatas,
hearing which we shall fulfill them in every aspect."
Then, Ānanda, that Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Lokeśvararāja,
having understood the intention of that bhikṣu,
[remained] for a full ten million years.

Out of desire for their welfare and seeking their benefit, he fully revealed, with its specific forms, details, and explanations, the excellence of the array of qualities and adornments of the buddha-fields of eighty-one hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of buddhas.
Out of compassion, having taken up compassion, for the sake of not interrupting the lineage of the Buddhas,
[he generated] great compassion toward sentient beings.
Having brought this about, the lifespan of that Blessed One was a full forty-two kalpas.
Then, Ānanda, that monk Dharmākara—those eighty-one [billion... of theirs...
Having taken up within a single buddha-field all those perfections of the arrays of the qualities and ornaments of the buddha-fields of hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of buddhas,
and having bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Lokeśvara, he said:
Having circumambulated him, he departed from the presence of that Blessed One. Furthermore,
for five kalpas thereafter, [he beheld] the perfect array of the qualities and ornaments of the Buddha-field.
And he has taken up [practices] that are more exalted and more sublime, which have never before been practiced in all the worlds throughout the ten directions;
And he made a sublime vow. Thus indeed, Ānanda, by that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja, [the vow was made] regarding those eighty-one hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of Buddha-fields.
The excellence [of the Buddha-fields] has been described;
having then taken hold of Buddha-field excellences that are superior to those, more sublime, and more immeasurable, [one attains them].
Having approached where that Tathāgata was,
he bowed his head at the feet of that Blessed One and said this:
He said: "Blessed One, I have taken hold of the perfection of the array of the ornaments and qualities of the buddha-field. When this had been said, Ānanda, [the Blessed One said:]
That Tathāgata, the Lord of the World King, said this to that monk:
"In that case, monk, speak."
The Tathāgata approves. This is the time, O Bhikṣu; gladden the assembly, produce joy, roar the lion’s roar, hearing which—
"Bodhisattvas, mahāsattvas, both now and in the future, will embrace such vows for the perfection of buddha-fields. Then, Ānanda, at that time, that monk Dharmākara—
He said this to the Blessed One:
"In that case, may the Blessed One listen to me regarding my particular vows."
Just as when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, that buddha-field shall be endowed with an array of inconceivable qualities and ornaments.
1. Blessed One, if in that buddha-field there should be hell, or the animal realm, or the domain of hungry ghosts, or the host of asuras, may it not be so; rather—
"May I awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
2. O Blessed One, if the sentient beings who are born there in that buddha-field..."
Furthermore, having passed away from there, they might fall into hell, or the animal realm, or the domain of hungry ghosts, or the body of an asura.
May I not attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment until this occurs:
O Blessed One, if all those beings who are reborn in that buddha-field of mine...
And may they all not be of a single color— namely, golden-colored; only then shall I attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
May I fully awaken.
4. O Blessed One, if in that buddha-field there should be perceived any distinction between gods and humans, except for the conventional designation of names—

"May I not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment as long as beings in that Buddha-field of mine are merely designated by the conventional usage of calculation and enumeration as 'gods' or 'humans.
5. O Blessed One, if in that Buddha-field those beings..."
If all of them were to be reborn there, yet they did not possess mastery over supernatural powers (ṛddhivaśitā) or have attained the supreme perfection (paramapāramitā),
such that they could traverse hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields even in the fraction of a single moment of thought;
May I not attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment so long as,
O Blessed One, those beings in that buddha-field of mine—
If they were to be reborn,
and if they all were not to possess the recollection of their past lives— even by way of remembering as many as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons— then [this would be so].
May I not attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment so long as,
O Blessed One, those beings in that buddha-field of mine—
If they were to be reborn, none of them would obtain the divine eye, not even to the extent of seeing hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of world-systems. Mā P12.
"May I not attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment until then.
O Blessed One, if those beings who would be reborn in that buddha-field of mine,"
May they all not obtain the divine ear,
even to the extent of hearing the true Dharma simultaneously from as far as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields.
May I not attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment so long as,
O Blessed One, there are sentient beings in that buddha-field of mine...
If they were to be reborn, none of them would become skilled in knowing the minds of others,
even regarding those included within hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddha-fields.
May I not first attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment until I have fully understood the mental conduct of sentient beings.
10. "If, Blessed One, those beings who would be reborn in that buddha-field should give rise to even the slightest notion of possession,"
Even with regard to my own body,
may I not first awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
11. "If, Blessed One, those beings who would be reborn in that buddha-field were not all destined for certainty, [may I not attain perfect enlightenment]."
Namely: from the state of rightness up until the great final nirvana,
let there not yet be [the attainment of] unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
May I fully awaken.
12. O Blessed One, if, when I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment in that buddha-field, [it should be so...]
Some being might attain [the state] among the assemblies of the śrāvakas,
even as far as the trichiliocosm—

Even if all sentient beings included within a great trichiliocosm were to become pratyekabuddhas and were to count for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of eons, may I not yet attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
13. "O Blessed One, if, when I have awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment,
my light in that buddha-field is not of a measurable magnitude, may I not attain it."
May I not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening, even if it were to take as long as hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of Buddha-fields.
14. Blessed One, if, when I have awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and attained awakening in that buddha-field,
the lifespan of sentient beings were to be measurable, with the exception of...
By the power of my vow, may I not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment for as long as [that time].

15. "If, O Blessed One, when I have attained awakening, my lifespan should have a limit— even by counting hundreds of thousands of nayutas of kotis of eons— may I not then realize unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
May I attain perfect enlightenment.
16. O Blessed One, may it be that when I have attained enlightenment, even the name of unwholesomeness should not exist among the beings in that buddha-field. May it not be so.
"May I not attain unexcelled, perfect enlightenment until [that time].
17. Blessed One, if, when I have attained enlightenment, among immeasurable..."
In immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields, the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, might proclaim his name,
yet they would not speak his praise.
They should not utter praise,
nor should they proclaim it.
May I not attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening until— O Blessed One— if, when I have attained awakening, [the following occurs]:
Those beings who, in other world-systems, having generated the mind set on unexcelled perfect enlightenment,
hear my name,
If those with serene minds should recollect me,
and if, when the time of their death has arrived, I were not to stand before them, surrounded and honored by the community of monks; that—
This is for the sake of non-distraction of the mind:
may I not, for the time being, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
19. "O Blessed One, if, when I have attained enlightenment, those beings in immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields who, having heard my name, should direct their minds toward that Buddha-field,"
and they were to dedicate their roots of merit toward rebirth there,
yet they were not to be reborn in that buddha-field;

Even in as few as ten cycles of generating the thought of awakening— excluding those beings who have committed the immediate transgressions and those obscured by the veil of rejecting the true Dharma.
"May I not attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment until [that time].
20. Blessed One, when I have attained enlightenment, in that buddha-field..."
If all those bodhisattvas were to be reborn,
yet none of them were endowed with the thirty-two marks of a great man, let that not be so.
"May I fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Blessed One, if, when I have attained enlightenment,
in that buddha-field..."
Whatever sentient beings might be reborn there,
they would all be bound to only one more birth before attaining unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Except for those very bodhisattva mahāsattvas who are clad in the great armor and possess specific vows.
Those who are armored for the sake of all the world, those who are dedicated to the welfare of all the world, and those who are dedicated to bringing about the final nirvana of all the world.
Those who desire to practice the conduct of a bodhisattva in all world-systems, those who desire to honor all Buddhas,
and [those who desire to save] sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges.
of those who establish others in unexcelled, perfect enlightenment;
and furthermore,
of those who are oriented toward the higher practice and are certain in the conduct of Samantabhadra— do not [despise them].
"May I not attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment until [that time].
22. Blessed One, when I have attained enlightenment, in that buddha-field..."
Whatever bodhisattvas might be reborn there, they would all, by means of a single morning meal, go to other buddha-fields.
many hundreds of Buddhas, many thousands of Buddhas,
many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas, many [millions]...
Even if there were ten million Buddhas,
or even many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of Buddhas, they would not remain present.
With all the requisites for happiness,
namely: by the power of the Buddhas,
may I not first realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment—
May I awaken.
23. O Blessed One, if, when I have attained awakening, in that buddha-field...
Whatever kinds of forms those bodhisattvas might desire to employ to gather roots of merit,
namely: with gold, or...
Or with silver,
or with any various jewels such as gems, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, crystals, coral, rock crystal, musāragalva, red pearls, emeralds, and so forth.
or with all kinds of flowers, perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols,
banners, flags, and lamps; or with all kinds of dance, song, and instrumental music— to them...
If such forms as these were not to manifest simultaneously with the arising of that thought, may I never attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
24. Blessed One, if, when I have attained enlightenment, [such things should not occur]...
In that buddha-field,
whatever sentient beings may be reborn, they shall all not be [devoid of] that which is accompanied by omniscience.
May they preach discourses on the Dharma; until then, may I not awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.

25. "O Blessed One, may it be so that when I have attained awakening, if such a thought should arise in the bodhisattvas in that buddha-field: [may they never think of returning to the world of saṃsāra]."
What if we, remaining right here in this world-system, were to honor, revere, and respect the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, in immeasurable and incalculable Buddha-fields? P16
We shall honor [him] with these:
robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, as well as flowers, incense, perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
With powdered incense, robes, parasols, banners, and flags; with various kinds of dance, song, and instrumental music;
and with rains of jewels—if those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, [respond] simultaneously with the arising of their thought...
They would not accept it, thinking: "Out of compassion,
may I first not [attain] unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening."
May I awaken.
26. O Blessed One, if, when I have attained awakening, in that buddha-field...
If there were bodhisattvas who had been reborn [there],

Of other trees, Ānanda, the roots are made of gold.
The trunks are made of silver,
the branches of beryl,
and the twigs of crystal.
The leaves were made of musāragalva,
the flowers were made of red pearls,
and the fruits were made of emerald.
Ānanda, some trees have roots made of silver, trunks made of beryl,
and [branches] made of crystal.
The trunks were made of emerald, the branches of musāragalva, the leaves of red pearl,
and the flowers of emerald.
The fruits are made of gold;
Ānanda, some trees have roots made of lapis lazuli and trunks made of crystal.
The trunks were made of emerald, the branches of red pearl,
and the leaves of emerald-garbha stone.
The flowers were made of gold and the fruits were made of silver; such,
Ānanda, were some of the trees.
The roots are made of crystal, the trunks are made of musāragalva,
and [the branches] are made of red pearls.
The trunks were made of emerald, the branches of emerald,
the leaves of gold, and the flowers of silver.
The fruits are made of lapis lazuli;
Ānanda, some trees have roots made of musāragalva and trunks made of red pearls.
The branches were made of emerald, the twigs of gold,
and the leaves of silver.
The flowers were made of beryl and the fruits were made of crystal; such,
Ānanda, were some of the trees.
The roots are made of red pearls,
the trunks are made of emerald,
and they are made of gold.
The trunks were made of gold, the branches of silver, the leaves of beryl,
and the flowers of crystal.
The fruits are made of musāragalva;
Ānanda, the roots of some trees are made of emerald (aśmagarbha),
while their trunks are made of gold.
The trunks were made of silver,
the branches of beryl,
and the leaves of crystal.
The flowers were made of musāragalva,
and the fruits were made of red pearls; such,
Ānanda, were some of the trees.
the roots consist of the seven precious gems,
the trunks consist of the seven precious gems,
and [the branches] consist of the seven precious gems.
The branches, the limbs made of the seven precious gems, the leaves made of the seven precious gems, and the flowers made of the seven precious gems.
The fruits consist of the seven precious gems.
And, Ānanda, the roots, trunks, branches, twigs, leaves, flowers, and fruits of all those trees are soft, pleasant to the touch, and fragrant; [this is] by means of the wind.
And from those trees, a beautiful and charming sound issues forth—
exquisite, not disagreeable to hear.
Ānanda, that place is completely covered with such trees made of the seven precious gems.
The buddha-field was surrounded on all sides by plantain trunks made of the seven precious gems and by rows of jewel-palm trees,
and it was entirely covered with nets of gold.
And it was covered on all sides with lotuses made of the seven precious gems;
among them were lotuses measuring half a yojana, and some measuring a full yojana.

There are [lotuses] measuring two, three, four, or five yojanas, and some even reaching ten yojanas in size. And from every jewel-lotus, thirty-six thousand koṭis of rays of light emanate. And from every [side],...
From the mouth of the ray issued thirty-six thousand koṭis of Buddhas, with bodies the color of gold and endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man,
who [appeared] in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the eastern direction.

Having gone there, they teach the Dharma to sentient beings. In this way, having gone to immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the southern, western, and northern directions, as well as below, above, and in the intermediate directions throughout the unobstructed world, they—
They teach the Dharma to sentient beings.
Furthermore, Ānanda, in that buddha-field there are no mountains of black iron at all.
There are no jewel mountains on all sides; there are no Sumerus, kings of mountains, on all sides;
and there are no Cakravāḍas or Mahācakravāḍas, [kings of mountains], on all sides.
There are no kings, nor are there great oceans. And that buddha-field is level and delightful on all sides, like the palm of a hand, with ground sections strewn with various kinds of jewels.

When this had been said, the venerable Ānanda spoke thus to the Blessed One: "Furthermore, Blessed One, as for those gods of the Four Great Kings who dwell on the slopes of Sumeru, or the Trāyastriṃśa gods who dwell on the summit of Sumeru..."
"Where are they established? The Blessed One said:
"What do you think, Ānanda? As for those Yāma gods and Tuṣita gods who are here upon Sumeru, the king of mountains..."
the gods, the gods who delight in emanation,
the gods who wield power over the emanations of others,
and the gods of the Brahma-realm.
the gods who are ministers of Brahmā,
the gods of Mahābrahmā, up to the Akaniṣṭha gods.
"Wherein are they established? He replied:
"O Blessed One, the ripening of karma and the formative activity of karma are inconceivable."
The Blessed One said:
"Ānanda, you have experienced the inconceivable ripening of karma, the formation of karma."

Furthermore, the inconceivable buddha-adhiṣṭhāna of the Blessed Buddhas is not [limited], nor is the inconceivable manifestation of merit there for those beings who have performed meritorious deeds and planted roots of virtue. He said:

"Blessed One, I have no doubt, nor uncertainty, nor hesitation regarding this matter. Nevertheless, for the sake of dispelling the doubt, uncertainty, and hesitation of future beings, I ask the Tathāgata about this point."
"I ask [this question]. The Blessed One said:
"Excellent, excellent, Ānanda! You should act in this way."
Indeed, Ānanda, in that world-system Sukhāvatī, rivers flow in various kinds. There are great rivers there one yojana in width; there are even those up to twenty, thirty, forty, and fifty [yojanas].
They extend for as much as a hundred thousand yojanas in width and are twelve yojanas in depth.
And all the rivers flowed pleasantly,
carrying waters fragrant with various sweet scents.
They carry clusters of flowers strewn with various jewels and resound with the cries of various sweet melodies. And of those, Ānanda, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of parts...
From the musical instruments, played by skilled musicians and resonating with divine music,
there issues forth such a charming sound as the sound that issues from those great rivers.
Profound, to be known, to be understood, and faultless.
Pleasant to the ear, heart-touching, lovely, and charmingly beautiful.
It is refreshing and not disagreeable; it is worth hearing, and because it concerns the inconceivable, the peaceful, and selflessness, it is pleasant to hear. P35
They come within the range of the sense of hearing of those beings.
Furthermore, Ānanda, on both sides of those great rivers—
The banks are covered with various fragrant trees,
from which various branches, leaves, flowers, and clusters of blossoms hang down. There, those beings who are on those riverbanks—
Desiring to experience divine, non-material pleasure and play,
as they enter those rivers while desiring [to bathe], [the water reaches] only up to their ankles.
The waters stand still for those who desire them to reach the height of the knees, the waist, or the armpits.
For those who desire it, water remains up to their necks,
and divine delights appear. There, whichever beings desire,
"May there be cool water," [it becomes so].
It becomes cool for those who desire it to become warm.
It becomes hot for those who desire:
"May it be cold and hot."
For them, that water becomes cool or warm according to their pleasure.
And those great rivers are scented with divine *tamāla* leaves, *agaru*, and *kālānusārin*, and are filled with the fragrance of *tagara* and serpents.
They flow filled with water scented by the finest fragrance of excellent sandalwood;
they are covered with divine flowers such as utpala, padma, kumuda, puṇḍarīka, and saugandhika, and [filled with] swans, cranes, ruddy geese, kāraṇḍava ducks, parrots, mynas, cuckoos, and kuṇālas.
Their sandy banks were frequented by flocks of birds manifested by the Tathāgata, such as kalaviṅkas and peacocks, possessing enchanting voices;
they were further adorned with the eight kinds of precious elements.
They have excellent landing-stairs,
are free from mud,
and are strewn with golden sand. There, when those beings...
When they desire, "May such intentions of ours be fulfilled," then those very same righteous intentions of theirs are fulfilled. (Yaś P36)
And, Ānanda, the sound of that water issues forth so delightful that it makes itself known throughout the entire buddha-field. There, those beings who stand on the riverbanks and desire [to hear it]:
"May this sound not come into the range of our auditory faculty," they thought;
yet it came into the range even of their divine auditory faculty.
It does not come. And whatever kind of sound each [being] desires to hear, that very kind of pleasant [sound] [arises].
He hears a sound;
for example,
the word "Buddha."
the word "Dharma," the word "Saṃgha," and the word "Pāramitā."
the word "ground," the word "power," and the word "fearlessness."
the sound of the unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇikabuddhadharma*),

the sound of the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the sound of the analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and [the sounds of] emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and lack of volitional effort (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
The sound of the unborn, the unarisen, non-existence, and cessation;
the sound of peace, perfect peace, and total tranquility; the sound of great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.

And they hear the sound of the attainment of the stage of consecration through the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). Having heard such sounds as these, they attain a sublime joy and rapture.
Accompanied by seclusion, accompanied by dispassion, and accompanied by peace.
It is accompanied by cessation,
accompanied by the Dharma, and accompanied by the roots of merit that bring about the perfection of enlightenment.
Furthermore, Ānanda, in the world-system Sukhāvatī, the word "unwholesome" does not exist in any way;
the word "hindrance" does not exist in any way; and [the words for] the states of woe, miserable destinies, and falling into ruin do not exist in any way.
The word "suffering" does not exist; in every respect, the word "suffering" does not exist;
[there is] neither-suffering-nor-happiness—
Even the word "feeling," Ānanda, does not exist there;
how much less, then, could there be suffering or the word "suffering"? P37
Therefore, Ānanda, by this method that world-system is called Sukhāvatī in brief,
but not in detail; even an eon would not suffice to reach its end.
One might go to the world-system Sukhāvatī while proclaiming the causes of happiness there;
yet it would not be possible to reach the end of those causes of happiness.
Furthermore, Ānanda, all those beings who have been born, or will be born, in that world-system Sukhāvatī,
are all of such a form.

In terms of complexion, strength, power, height and girth, sovereignty, accumulation of merit, and supernormal knowledges, [he was endowed with] garments, ornaments, gardens, celestial palaces, and gabled chambers.
They were endowed with enjoyments, such as the enjoyment of sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles of such a kind, and possessed all such articles of use and enjoyment; that—
Just as, for example, the gods who wield power over the creations of others;
furthermore, Ānanda, the beings in the world-system Sukhāvatī do not consume coarse, solid food. Rather, indeed, they...
Whatever kind of food they desire, that very kind they perceive as having been brought;
and their bodies become refreshed.
Their bodies are gratified; no further application [of ointment] needs to be made to their bodies. With their bodies thus gratified, they desire such kinds of fragrances as these.
That entire buddha-field is perfumed by such divine varieties of incense.
Therein, whoever does not wish to smell that fragrance, [does not smell it].

In him, even the latent impression of the perception of any odor whatsoever does not manifest. Likewise, those who desire such things as perfumes, garlands, ointments, powders, robes, parasols, banners, flags, and musical instruments— [none of these manifest for him].
By means of such forms as these, that entire buddha-field becomes completely filled for them.
Whatever robes of various colors and many hundreds of kinds they desire— P38.
They possess a thousand colors,
and that buddha-field becomes completely filled with such precious robes as those.
They perceive themselves as already clothed;
whatever kinds of ornaments they desire, [they obtain].
For example: head ornaments,
or ear ornaments,
or ornaments for the neck, hands, and feet.
Or, namely: crowns, earrings,
bracelets, and armlets.
A necklace of calf-tooth beads,
a necklace of gold coins,
and an ear-ornament.
finger-rings, golden threads, girdles, and golden nets;
All the networks of jewel bracelets were clearly adorned with such ornaments, inlaid with hundreds of thousands of various gems.
They beheld that buddha-field as follows:
they perceived themselves adorned with those very ornaments, garments, and jewel-trees.
Whatever kind of celestial palace they desire—
whatever its color, mark, and shape, and whatever its height and circumference— [they obtain].
It was adorned with hundreds of thousands of turrets made of various jewels,
and strewn with diverse celestial cloths.
A celestial palace exactly like that, with jeweled couches arranged upon variegated cushions, [appeared] for them.
They appear before them. When those palaces have been manifested by their minds, they dwell within them, surrounded and honored by seven thousand apsarases;
they play, enjoy themselves, and amuse themselves.
And in that world-system there is no diversity among gods or humans; except by way of conventional usage, they are designated as "gods" or "humans. It is just so, Ānanda.
In the presence of a universal monarch,
one who is deficient among men, a eunuch, does not shine nor does he glow.
He does not shine,
he is not confident,
and he is not radiant.
In the same way, in the presence of the gods of the Heaven of Controlling Others' Emanations (paranirmitavaśavartin), Śakra, the lord of the gods, does not shine,
does not glow, and does not radiate.
Namely: by means of gardens, celestial palaces, garments, and ornaments;
or by sovereignty; or by supernatural power.
[They do so] either by means of a miraculous display or by means of sovereign power; but certainly not through the realization of the Dharma or the enjoyment of the Dharma.
In this regard, Ānanda, it is like the gods who wield power over the creations of others.
In this way, the humans in the world-system Sukhāvatī are to be regarded.
Furthermore, Ānanda, when the time of the forenoon has arrived in that world-system Sukhāvatī,
From all sides and in the four directions, tumultuous winds blow,
by which these variegated jewel-trees here—
beautiful to behold, of various colors,
and of many colors.
They agitate and thoroughly stir up the waters, which are perfumed by various divine and fragrant scents.
They cause them to move, they cause them to move together; from which many hundreds of flowers [arise] upon that jewel-encrusted earth.
Pleasant-smelling and beautiful flowers fall down. By those flowers, that buddha-field becomes adorned on all sides to the height of seven men.
It is just as if some man were skillful...
One should spread a carpet of flowers upon the earth, arranging them evenly with both hands so that it is most wonderful and beautiful to behold; in this same way,
this Buddha-field is completely covered on all sides by those flowers of various fragrances and colors.
It becomes clearly seven fathoms high. And those varieties of flowers are soft, with a pleasant touch like that of kācalindika cloth;
they are merely comparable to what is placed [upon them].
When the foot is lowered, it sinks down exactly four finger-breadths;
when the foot is lifted, it rises back up exactly four finger-breadths. Then, when the time of the forenoon had passed, they emerged.
Those flowers vanished without remainder.
Then that buddha-field became secluded.
It becomes delightful and auspicious through those previously offered flowers that have not decayed. Then, once again,
winds blow from all four directions.
Those who, as before, scatter fresh flowers— at the time of forenoon, at midday, and at afternoon— just as they did previously.
at twilight, during the first watch of the night,
and during the middle and last watches; and by those winds as they blow.
When those beings were touched by [the breezes] perfumed with various fragrances,
they became so endowed with bliss that it was as if they had entered the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpanna*).
Ānanda, in that buddha-field,
the very names of fire, moon, sun, planets, lunar mansions, and the forms of stars, as well as of blinding darkness, will not exist in any way whatsoever.

Even designation does not exist; in every respect, even the designation of night and day does not exist, except for the conventional usage of the Tathāgata. And in every respect, the notion of possession of a house does not exist.
Furthermore, Ānanda, at that time in that world-system Sukhāvatī, clouds of divine scented water rain down, as do celestial flowers of every color.
Divine seven-jeweled treasures,
divine sandalwood powder, and divine parasols, banners, and flags rain down. Divine...
Celestial palaces and divine canopies are sustained;
divine jeweled parasols with fly-whisks are held in the sky; and divine musical instruments are played.
And divine apsarases danced.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those beings who have been born, are being born, or will be born in that buddha-field—
All of them are destined for rightness until they reach nirvāṇa. For what reason? Because therein there is no establishment or designation of two groups.
Namely: those who are not fixed [in destiny] or those who are fixed in falsehood. Therefore, Ānanda, by this method as well, that world-system is called Sukhāvatī in brief.
Not in detail.
Even an eon, Ānanda, would be exhausted in describing the world-system Sukhāvatī.
While the causes of happiness are being proclaimed,
it is not possible to reach the end of those causes of happiness.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"May all sentient beings indeed become Sugatas."
Those of pure knowledge, skilled in the ultimate truth,
might for ten million eons, or even longer,
proclaim the description of Sukhāvatī. (1)
Even if they were to travel for tens of millions of eons,
there would be no end to the description of Sukhāvatī;
their eloquence would never come to an end.
Then the garland of phonemes, illuminating them,
would cut through, break apart, and reduce to dust those world-systems that are as numerous as atoms.
Therefore, even if one were to fill many world-systems beyond measure and give them as a gift of jewels,
it would not equal even a fraction, nor could it be compared to that [merit].
The world-systems become vast through merit;
for even by merely hearing the name of the world-system Sukhāvatī here, such merit is produced. (4)
Then there would be great merit for those who have faith in what is designated as the word of the Jina;
for faith is indeed the root for attaining the world's goal.
"Therefore, having heard this, one should dispel doubt.
(5) Thus, Ānanda, the world-system Sukhāvatī possesses such immeasurable praise of its qualities.
Furthermore, Ānanda, regarding that Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitābha—P42...
In each of the ten directions, in Buddha-fields as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, Buddhas, Blessed Ones, as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges, proclaim his name.
They speak their praise, proclaim their fame, and extol their virtues. For what reason? Because those who...
Some beings hear the name of that Tathāgata Amitābha, and having heard it, they produce even a single thought of resolve accompanied by serene faith through their deep aspiration.
They all abide in the state of non-retrogression regarding unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
And those beings whatsoever, Ānanda, who [repeatedly] [approach] that Tathāgata...
They will attend to it according to its aspects and will plant a vast and immeasurable root of merit.
Having dedicated their minds toward enlightenment and made a vow to be reborn in that world-system,
Amitābha will [welcome] them.
When the time of death has arrived, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, will remain there, surrounded and honored by a multitude of many monks.
Then, upon seeing that Blessed One, they will have minds full of serene faith right then and there.
One is reborn in the world-system of Sukhāvatī. Ānanda, whatever son of good family or daughter of good family should desire:
"How might I, in this very life..."
Thinking, "May I behold that Tathāgata Amitābha," he should generate the mind set on unexcelled, perfect enlightenment with a mental continuum inclined toward the resolute intention (*adhyāśaya*).
Having directed one's mind toward that buddha-field for the sake of rebirth there, one should dedicate the roots of virtue.
Furthermore, those who will no longer bring that Tathāgata to mind...
And those who will repeatedly plant vast and immeasurable roots of merit,
and direct their minds toward that buddha-field—
for them, that Tathāgata Amitābha, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, [will appear] in just such a manner.
With the same complexion, physical form, height, and girth, and surrounded by a community of monks,

an emanation of the Buddha will stand before them at the time of death; through that very concentration which takes as its object the serene faith born from seeing the Tathāgata, they shall remain undeluded.
Having passed away from there through mindfulness, they will be reborn right in that same buddha-field.
Furthermore, Ānanda, those beings who [direct their thoughts] toward that Tathāgata for ten moments of thought...
They will remember [it];
they will conceive a longing for that buddha-field; and they will feel satisfaction when profound dharmas are being taught.
They will attain it;
they will not fail;
they will not fall into despondency.
They will fall into ruin;
yet, even for a single moment of thought, they will bring that Tathāgata to mind.
And those who shall conceive a longing for that buddha-field will, even while in their dreams, behold that Tathāgata Amitābha;
they too shall be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī.
"And they shall become irreversible from unexcelled, perfect enlightenment. Indeed, Ānanda, it is by perceiving this very purpose that [the Tathāgata acts]."
Those Tathāgatas,
in immeasurable and incalculable world-systems in the ten directions, proclaim the name and praise the qualities of that Tathāgata Amitābha.
Proclaiming it, they utter words of praise. Furthermore, Ānanda, in that buddha-field, from each of the ten directions—
In that direction, Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the river Ganges approach that Tathāgata Amitābha in order to behold him and pay him homage.
for the purpose of attending upon him and for the purpose of questioning him;
and that assembly of bodhisattvas and those...
and to behold the specific excellences of the array of ornaments and qualities of the Buddha-fields.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One, in order to further elucidate this very matter, spoke these verses: P44: [The verses follow]
Just as there are grains of sand in the river Ganges,
so many were the buddha-fields from which they came to pay homage to the Buddha.
Those bodhisattvas took many handfuls of flowers— of various colors, fragrant, and delightful— to offer to the Leader Amitāyus.
They sprinkle [offerings] upon the supreme leader of men, the one of immeasurable life who is honored by gods and humans;
likewise in the south, west, and north. (2)
As many Buddha-fields as there are in the ten directions, from each of those places the bodhisattvas have come to pay homage to the Leader Amitāyus. (3)
Taking many bundles of fragrances— variegated, sweet-smelling, and delightful—
they scatter them over the Supreme Leader of Men.
Having honored those many bodhisattvas, who are revered by gods and men for their immeasurable life, and having paid homage at the feet of Amitaprabha, (4) [he departed].
Having circumambulated [him], they spoke thus:
"Oh, how wonderful! This Buddha-field shines with splendor.
They scattered handfuls of flowers over him.
With uplifted minds and incomparable joy, they spoke these words again to the Leader: "May our field also become like this. (6) P45
When they threw those flower-baskets there, they then became a parasol extending for a hundred yojanas; well-adorned and with a variegated handle, it shone brilliantly.
They cover the Buddha’s entire body.
Having thus honored him, those bodhisattvas engage in conversation, and he is delighted by that.
Truly, those beings have gained a well-attained benefit who have heard the name of the Supreme among Men;
we too have previously gained a well-attained benefit. (8)
Since you have come to this buddha-field,
behold what kind of field it is— resembling a dream—
which was fashioned by the Teacher over a thousand eons. (9)
Behold, the Buddha, a supreme mass of merit,
shines resplendent, surrounded by bodhisattvas; infinite is the radiance of Amitābha and infinite his splendor.
The lifespan is immeasurable, and the Saṅgha is immeasurable.
O Lord Amitāyus, you who manifest a smile!
Thirty-six quintillion rays of light, having issued forth from the circle of his face, illuminate thousands of millions of buddha-fields. (11)
All those rays returned there and vanished into the crown of the Leader’s head. Gods and humans were filled with joy. P46.
Then, perceiving that the radiance had set,
the son of the Buddha of great renown rose up;
he was indeed named Avalokiteśvara.
What is the cause here, O Blessed One, what is the condition, by which you, O Lord of the World, manifest a smile? (13)
May you, who are skilled in the ultimate truth, compassionate toward the welfare of others, and the liberator of many beings, explain that;
having heard those most excellent and delightful words, [I shall understand].
Those bodhisattvas in many world-systems who have set out for Sukhāvatī in order to behold the Buddha will become beings with uplifted minds. (14)
Having heard this and generated vast joy,
they would quickly behold this field;
and having come to this sublime field, (15)
He quickly attained the power of supernatural faculties,
as well as the divine eye and likewise the divine ear.
Remembering his past lives and skilled in the highest doctrines,
Amitāyus Buddha then prophesied:
"For this was my vow in the past."
"How might sentient beings, upon hearing my name,
always go to my field?"—
this beautiful aspiration of mine has been fulfilled. (17)
And beings come from many world-systems;
having arrived quickly into my presence, they become non-retrogressive here, destined for only one more birth. (18)
Therefore, whatever bodhisattva here desires:
"May my field also be of such a kind;
may I too liberate many beings," P47.
By name, by sound, and by sight—
let him go very swiftly, in a state of great haste, to the world-realm Sukhāvatī.
Having first gone to Amitaprabha,
he shall worship ten million billion Buddhas; having worshipped many billions of Buddhas, (20) [he shall proceed].

Having traveled to many fields by the power of their supernormal abilities and having performed worship in the presence of the Sugatas, they will come to Sukhāvatī as the foremost of those who have offered food. (21)
Furthermore, Ānanda, the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One, the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha Amitāyus, is sixteen hundred yojanas in height,
with its branches, leaves, and foliage extending eight hundred yojanas downward.
It has a height and circumference of five hundred yojanas at its base;
it is always leafy, always flowering, and always bearing fruit.
It was of various colors, possessing many hundreds of thousands of colors;
it had various leaves, various flowers, and various fruits,
and was beautifully adorned with various diverse forms.
It was completely covered with moonlight-like maṇi-jewels,
variegated with Śakrābhilagna maṇi-jewels, and strewn with wish-fulfilling cintāmaṇi jewels.
It was exquisitely adorned with the finest jewels from the great ocean,
surpassing those of the divine realms,
and hung with threads of gold.
A necklace of gold coins, a necklace of jewels, a necklace of diamonds, a necklace of bracelets, a necklace of red pearls, and a necklace of blue pearls.
Adorned with hundreds of all-jeweled bodices, with girdles of *siṃhalatā* vines and jeweled threads,
and with nets of gold and nets of pearls; [and] with all kinds of jewels...
It was adorned with a network of small bells,
and embellished with sea-monsters, svastikas, nandyāvartas, and half-moons.
It was adorned with ornaments of all kinds of jewels, gold, and precious gems, such as tinkling bells,
and it was further embellished according to the mental inclinations and perceptions of sentient beings.
Moreover, Ānanda, when that Bodhi tree was stirred by the wind...
Whatever sound issues forth makes itself known throughout immeasurable world-systems. In that regard, Ānanda, for those beings to whom the sound of the Bodhi tree [reaches]... P48
When [this] comes within the range of their hearing,

they have no perception of "otherness," nor do they have a perception of "self."

With minds of loving-kindness, with gentle minds, and with affectionate minds.
With pliant minds,

and they were equal to the ocean in their wisdom.
Equal to Mount Meru in wisdom, she is a repository of manifold virtues;

accomplishing, teaching, illuminating, and expanding upon the Buddha-eye.

With tamed minds,
with peaceful minds,

They were endowed with [these qualities],

Skilled in what is beneficial and what is not, and skilled in the principles of right and wrong conduct,

They attain confidence; they are skilled in the investigation of all phenomena,
they dwell in the knowledge of the natural quiescence of the nature of all phenomena, and their sphere of activity is non-apprehension.
Possessing nothing, free from grasping, and free from anxiety.
Free from distress,
completely liberated without grasping,
stainless, and abiding without limit.
Abiding without root in the superknowledges,
with unattached minds, and undaunted.
They apply themselves to profound dharmas and do not sink into despondency; they have emerged through entry into the Buddha-knowledge that is difficult to awaken to,
and they have attained the path of the single vehicle.
Free from doubt, having crossed over all hesitation,
and possessing knowledge that does not depend on others.
Free from conceit;
exalted in wisdom like Mount Sumeru;
equal to the ocean.
Unshakeable in intellect;
surpassing the radiance of the moon and sun through wisdom, and possessing a mind that is pure, bright white, and auspicious.
And because they possess the quality of radiance resembling the luster of refined gold;
and because they resemble the earth in supporting all sentient beings.
By way of casting off the auspicious and the inauspicious;
they are like water by way of being a flowing stream that washes away the accumulation of the stains of all afflictions.

they are like noble thoroughbred horses.

They are like birds because they take their stand upon the accumulation [of merit], and they are like the king of the twice-born Garuḍas because they are preceded by the sovereign power of all roots of goodness and dharmas.
Because it destroys the arguments of opposing disputants;

The dwelling in the womb of humans within noble lotuses. He said:

Whether they be fifty yojanas,

or seek out those who might liberate him from that prison.

Having turned back ninety-nine hundred thousand nayutas of kotis of kalpas,
they will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī;
from the presence of the Tathāgata Jvalanādhipati, twelve koṭis of bodhisattvas [will depart].
They will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī;
from the presence of the Tathāgata who has attained fearlessness, sixty-nine koṭis of bodhisattvas will be reborn in the world-system Sukhāvatī.
In order to behold, pay homage to, attend upon, inquire of, and question the Tathāgata Amitābha—
by this method, Ājita, their names are recited for a full hundred thousand million billion eons.
I would proclaim the names of those Tathāgatas from whom those bodhisattvas approach that Sukhāvatī world-system and that Amitābha.
To see, pay homage to, and attend upon the Tathāgata, it is not possible to reach the end [of those who do so].

Behold, Ajita, how great a gain have those beings obtained who shall hear the name of the Tathāgata Amitābha, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One; nor shall those beings be of inferior inclination.
Those who shall obtain even a single thought of serene faith toward that Tathāgata and toward this Dharma-discourse—
for that reason, then, Ajita;
I announce to you, I declare to you:
for the sake of hearing this Dharma-discourse in the presence of the world with its gods. P63
Even having plunged through and crossed over a trichiliocosm world-system filled with fire, one should not feel even a single moment of regret for the arising of a thought [of awakening].
Why is that? Because, O Ajita, it is due to not hearing these [teachings] that millions of bodhisattvas [fall away].
Such dharma-discourses turn one away from unexcelled,
perfect enlightenment. Therefore, for the sake of hearing, taking up, retaining, and understanding this dharma-discourse with a resolute intention, [one should listen].
for the sake of mastery,
for the purpose of explaining in detail,
and for the purpose of cultivation.
One must exert very great vigor; even for a single night or day,
or at least for the duration of a single milking of a cow.
Even having transcribed it into a book, it should be well-written and preserved;
and one should generate the perception of the Teacher toward it.
Those who desire to quickly establish immeasurable sentient beings in non-retrogression regarding unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment,
and [to reach] that buddha-field of the Blessed One, the Tathāgata Amitābha—
To behold [it], and to acquire for themselves a preeminent perfection of the array of qualities adorning their own buddha-field.
Moreover, Ajita;
Those beings have most excellently obtained their gain; they have planted roots of merit and have performed services for previous Victors.
And they shall be sustained by the empowerment of the Buddha,
for those who, in a future time, until—
While the destruction of the true Dharma is occurring, these very kinds of sublime Dharma discourses—
praised by all Buddhas and extolled by all Buddhas— [are being taught].
Authorized by all the Buddhas,
they are the swift bringers of the great, omniscient gnosis.
They will come within the range of their hearing; and having heard it, they will obtain sublime joy and gladness,
and will take it up.
They will uphold it, recite it, and master it.
And they will proclaim it in detail to others,
and they will delight in its cultivation, even to the extent of writing it down.
They will worship it and generate much merit, the measure of which is not easy to calculate.
Thus, Ajita, that which was to be done by the Tathāgata has been done by me. You must now apply yourselves with freedom from doubt.
Do not harbor uncertainty regarding the unattached and unobstructed wisdom of a Buddha; let it not be that [you lack] that which is endowed with all excellent modes.
Entering the dwelling of the nāga, bound by lotuses made of jewels. For, Ajita, the arising of a Buddha is difficult to encounter;
the teaching of the Dharma is difficult to encounter; [the opportunity for practice] is difficult to encounter.
The perfection of the opportune moment. Ajita, I have already explained how the perfection of former roots of merit was attained;
you should now apply yourselves and practice accordingly.
Furthermore, Ajita, this Dharma discourse is of great [merit].
I entrust this to you so that it may not perish. Do not strive for the disappearance of the Buddha-dharmas; do not disturb the command of the Tathāgata.
Then, at that time, the Blessed One spoke these verses:
"Such sounds as these will not be heard by those who have not performed meritorious deeds."
But those heroes who have accomplished their purpose shall hear these words,
for by them the Perfectly Awakened One, the Lord of the World, the Illuminator, has been seen.
That Dharma heard with reverence will bring you supreme joy;
it cannot be attained by those who are inferior or who hold wrong views.
To find faith in the teachings of the Buddhas— those who have performed worship for previous Buddhas shall train in the conduct of the Protectors of the World. (3)
Just as a man without eyes in the darkness does not know the path, so how could he show it?
In the same way, all the śrāvakas [are ignorant] regarding the Buddha-knowledge.
How much less so other beings, who are ignorant?
For only a Buddha understands the qualities of a Buddha;
neither gods, nāgas, asuras, yakṣas, nor śrāvakas can do so.
What would be the destination even of the Pratyekabuddhas, when the wisdom of the Buddha is being revealed? For if all sentient beings were to become Sugatas... (5)
Those who possess pure knowledge and are supremely skilled might, for ten million eons or even more, recount the virtues of a single Buddha. (6)
In the meantime, they might pass into nirvana while this is being proclaimed for many millions of eons,
yet no measure of the Buddha's wisdom can be found.
For such is the range of the knowledge of the Victors.
Therefore, a wise man of discerning nature who should place his faith in my words—
That witness, the Buddha, who is a mass of the Victor’s wisdom, fully understands and might utter [this] in words.
(8) Only rarely is the attainment of human birth obtained.
The appearance of Buddhas occurs only occasionally;
faith and wisdom are gained only after a very long time.
Therefore, those who possess the wisdom for this goal, you must generate diligence. (9)
Those who, having heard such a sublime Dharma,
obtain joy while recollecting the Sugata,
were our friends in the past.
"Those Buddhas who generate the aspiration for awakening...
(10). Now, while this Dharma discourse was being spoken by the Blessed One, the dust-free and stainless Dharma-eye regarding all phenomena arose in twelve *nayuta-koti* of beings.
The Dharma-eye was purified;
twenty-four koṭis attained the fruit of non-returning,
and eight hundred bhikṣus were liberated from the outflows through the realization of non-arising.

The minds were liberated. Twenty-five koṭis of bodhisattvas attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). And for four hundred thousand nayutas of koṭis of beings among gods and humans, [the seeds of] the non-arising [of outflows] were first produced.
They have generated the minds set upon unexcelled, perfect enlightenment and have planted roots of merit for rebirth in Sukhāvatī, out of a desire to behold the Blessed One Amitābha.

Having been born there in succession, they will all become Tathāgatas named Mañjusvara and arise in other world-systems. Furthermore, eighty nayuta-koṭis of beings who had attained patient acceptance under the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara became irreversible from unexcelled [enlightenment].
They were matured for perfect enlightenment by the Tathāgata Amitāyus himself while they were practicing their former bodhisattva conduct.
And having been reborn in the world-system of Sukhāvatī, they will fulfill their former practices of the original vows.
And at that time, this trichiliocosm great thousandfold world-system—
The earth shook in six ways, various miracles were manifested,
and the ground was covered knee-deep with mandārava flowers.
It was strewn [with flowers], and divine and human musical instruments were played in concert. And by the sound of the word "rejoicing," the entire realm up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven was made known.
The Blessed One spoke thus, and Ajita the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva and the Venerable Ānanda were uplifted with joy.
And that entire assembly,
including the world of gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced in what the Blessed One had spoken.

This is the proclamation of the virtues of the Blessed One Amitābha and the entry of the bodhisattvas into the stage of non-retrogression. The chapter on the array of Sukhāvatī of Amitābha is completed.
